To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) the free energy decomposition scheme was not successful at predicting binding affinilities of trypsin/ligand complexes, and 2) LISA, a linear empirical scoring function trained on a database of protein-ligand complexes, yielded good predictions in the SAMPL 3 challenge.

(a) the free energy decomposition method was able to achieve the lowest RMS error of any submitted method, and (b) the LISA score, with the inclusion of a classification step, was the most accurate in terms of RMS errors, with the best model yielding a 1.1 log-unit error.

1) the free energy decomposition scheme is a promising approach for predicting the binding affinity of small molecules to proteins, but it requires careful selection of parameters and training data; and 2) empirical scoring methods can provide good predictions of protein/ligands binding affinity if they are properly trained on relevant data.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the prediction of binding affinities and poses of small molecules to a protein target, trypsin.
the development and application of methods to estimate the affinities of molecular fragments binding to trypsin.
the prediction of the binding affinity of small organic molecules to the proteolytic enzyme trypsin.

the best models were those that used a combination of both training data and free energy decomposition.

the best predictions of binding affinities are obtained by using training data to scale raw scores.
the best predictions are made by methods which use training sets to estimate scaling parameters, and that the most accurate predictions were achieved by a combination of several different methods.
the best predictions are obtained when using a combination of physics-based and empirical models.
